opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the distinction is a lot thinner than people tend to assume. At a structural level, an eval and an RL environment are almost the same object. You have some distribution of tasks or prompts, a way for the model to interact with the task (maybe a single turn, maybe a multi-turn harness with tools), and a way of scoring what comes out. In an eval you take that score and report it as a number. In an RL environment you take that score and feed it back as a reward signal to update the model. The core machinery is shared: the task set, the interaction protocol, and the grader or rubric.

Where they start to diverge is in what you're optimizing for when you design them. With an eval, you mostly care that the measurement is meaningful and hard to game *as a measurement*. You want it to discriminate between models and to correlate with something people actually care about. You don't need it to be smooth or to give partial credit in a nice way, and it can be tiny. A few hundred carefully chosen problems can be a great eval.

For an RL environment, you care about a different set of properties. You need the reward to be learnable, which means the model should sometimes succeed and sometimes fail. If it's always zero or always one, there's no signal. You need enough diversity and volume that the model learns the skill rather than memorizing the tasks. And you have to be much more paranoid about reward hacking, because now you have an optimizer actively searching for whatever makes the number go up. A grader that's fine for reporting a benchmark score can fall apart once a policy is trained against it for thousands of steps.

So the way I like to put it: an eval is an environment you only run forward, and an environment is an eval you're willing to put optimization pressure on. That framing is useful in practice. It means that if you've built a good eval, with a clean harness, a clear task spec, and a reliable verifier, you've done a large part of the work of building an environment. It also means the open-source community can contribute to RL in a way that looks a lot like what people already do when they build benchmarks. That's a big part of why we've pushed toward a shared spec, where the same environment can be used for evaluation, for generating synthetic data, or for actual RL training without rewriting everything.

The caveat is the one I mentioned: optimization pressure changes things. Once you train on it, it's no longer a clean held-out measurement, and any weaknesses in the rubric will get found. So you still want separate held-out evals, but the gap between the two is much more about how you use them than what they fundamentally are.

r001.rationale: It says an evaluation score can be fed back as a reward to update the model, making the distinction largely about how the shared setup is used.

r002.rationale: It describes an evaluation as running tasks forward and reporting a score, while using that score to update the model belongs to RL.

r003.rationale: It describes reward-driven model updates and an optimizer searching against the grader over thousands of training steps, conveying performance-guided iteration at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that they're almost the same object, and the distinction is mostly about what you do with it rather than what it is.

An eval, at its core, is a set of tasks plus a way of scoring them. You give the model a problem, it produces something, and some function tells you how well it did. An RL environment is also a set of tasks plus a way of scoring them. The difference is that in the eval case you're just reading off the number, and in the RL case you're feeding that number back as a training signal. So structurally, an environment is an eval with a reward function attached, and an eval is an environment where you've decided not to update the weights.

That said, there are a few places where the two pull apart in practice. One is interactivity. A lot of classic evals are single-turn: here's a prompt, here's the answer, grade it. Environments tend to be multi-step. The model takes an action, the world responds, the model takes another action, and you only get a score at the end or along the way. So environments usually need some notion of state and a loop, whereas evals often don't.

Another is what you need the scoring to be robust against. With an eval, if the grader has a small bug or an exploitable edge case, it mostly just adds noise to your leaderboard. With an environment, the model is actively optimizing against that grader, so any crack in it will get found. Reward hacking is really just the discovery that your eval had a hole in it, and the model fell into the hole because you were pushing it in that direction. So environments have a much higher bar on the reward design side. You have to think adversarially about the thing you're measuring in a way that eval authors have historically not had to.

And then there's the question of scale and diversity. An eval can be a few hundred carefully curated examples, because you only need enough signal to compare models. An environment that you want to train on needs enough breadth that the model learns a general skill rather than memorizing the specific items. So you often end up with procedural generation, or verifiable tasks where you can produce as many instances as you want.

The way I tend to frame it to people is: every good environment is a good eval, but not every good eval is a good environment. The eval is the easier artifact. Once you've got one that's hard, well-specified, and resistant to shortcuts, turning it into an environment is mostly plumbing. The hard part was always deciding what you actually care about measuring and writing it down in a way that can't be gamed.

r001.rationale: The response says an environment feeds its score back as a training signal, blurring the distinction with an evaluation.

r002.rationale: It describes an evaluation as an environment where the score is read without updating model weights.

r003.rationale: It mentions using scores as training signals but does not characterize RL as automating performance-guided iteration at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is mostly in how you use it. An evaluation gives you a way to measure how well a model does on some task. A reinforcement learning environment gives the model something to interact with and a reward signal that you can use to improve it.

So the same task can serve both purposes. If you have a coding problem with tests, you can use those tests to evaluate whether the model solved it, or you can use passing the tests as a reward during training. The task itself hasn’t necessarily changed; what’s changed is whether you’re measuring the model or optimizing it.

The important thing is preserving some independent measurement. Once you start training against an evaluation, performance on it becomes evidence that you’re getting better at that training task. You still need held-out evaluations to understand whether that improvement generalizes.

r001.rationale: It says the same task can be used to measure performance or provide a reward during training, explaining how evaluation and training uses can blur.

r002.rationale: It defines evaluation as measuring how well a model performs and contrasts that with an environment used to improve the model.

r003.rationale: It describes using rewards to improve a model but does not characterize reinforcement learning as automating performance-guided iteration at scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of an evaluation as a way of measuring what a model can do, and a reinforcement learning environment as something the model can interact with to get better. You give it a task, it takes actions, and there’s some signal about how well it did.

The interesting thing is that those can be almost the same piece of software. If you have an evaluation where you can reliably score success, you can potentially train against it. The distinction is how you use it: are you updating the model based on those results, or are you holding it out to see whether the model has learned something that generalizes?

And an environment doesn’t necessarily have to be a rich simulation. It could be a math problem with a verifiable answer. But for longer tasks, it might include tools, intermediate observations, and consequences for the model’s actions. Then you’re testing—or training—not just whether it knows an answer, but whether it can figure out how to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says a reliably scored evaluation can be used for training and distinguishes evaluation from training by whether results update the model.

r002.rationale: It defines an evaluation as measuring what a model can do, while describing an RL environment as something the model interacts with to improve.

r003.rationale: It describes using results to train, but does not characterize reinforcement learning as automating performance-guided iteration at scale.
